p.src: This lyric, set to the tune “Nan Ke Zi,” tells only how the Tang Monk escaped the icy calamity of the Heaven-Reaching River and reached the farther shore upon the back of the great white soft-shelled turtle. Master and three disciples followed the main road and journeyed westward. It was the depths of winter: the dim light of the woods faded amid the mist, while the stark bones of the mountains rose sharp and clear beyond the waters.

u.src: This lyric, set to the tune “Nan Ke Zi,” tells only how the Tang Monk escaped the icy calamity of the Heaven-Reaching River and reached the farther shore upon the back of the great white soft-shelled turtle.
Master and three disciples followed the main road and journeyed westward.
It was the depths of winter: the dim light of the woods faded amid the mist, while the stark bones of the mountains rose sharp and clear beyond the waters.

p.src: As master and disciples travelled on, they suddenly came upon another great mountain blocking their way. The path was narrow, the cliffs high, and the rocky ridges steep; neither men nor horse could easily advance. Sanzang reined in his horse and called, “Disciples.” Sun Wukong at once led Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk forward to stand in attendance. “Master, what are your instructions?” they asked. Sanzang said, “Look how high the mountain ahead is. I fear there may be tigers and wolves working mischief, or monstrous beasts that harm travellers. This time you must be especially careful!” Wukong said, “Set your mind at ease, Master, and do not worry. We three brothers are united in heart and purpose, committed to the true path in our search for truth. Once we employ our arts for sweeping away monsters and subduing demons, what need have we to fear tigers, wolves, or monstrous beasts?” Hearing this, Sanzang could only set aside his fears and continue onward. At the mouth of a valley, he urged his horse up a cliff and raised his head to look carefully. What a splendid mountain it was:

p.src: Master and disciples braved the snow and bitter cold, shivering as they crossed the lofty peaks and rugged ridges. In the distance they saw tall towers rising from a hollow in the mountain, with quiet, secluded dwellings below. The Tang Monk said happily from horseback, “Disciples, we have been hungry and cold all day. Fortunately there are towers and houses in that mountain hollow. They must surely belong to some farming household, convent, Daoist abbey, or Buddhist monastery. Let us go and beg a little vegetarian food, eat, and then continue our journey.” Hearing this, Wukong swiftly opened his fiery eyes and looked. Over that place he saw baleful clouds looming and evil vapours seething. Turning back to the Tang Monk, he said, “Master, that is no wholesome place.” Sanzang said, “There are plainly towers, pavilions, and buildings there. How can it not be a wholesome place?” Wukong laughed. “Master, there is much you do not know. The road to the West is full of monsters and evil spirits skilled at conjuring country estates. They can conjure any towers, houses, halls, galleries, or pavilions they please to deceive people. You know the saying that the dragon has nine kinds of offspring; among them is one called the shen. When the shen’s breath gleams, it resembles towers and shallow pools. When great rivers lie dim and shrouded, the shen displays just such a spectacle. If birds and magpies happen to fly over, they are sure to come down and rest their wings. Whether they number thousands or tens of thousands, it swallows them all in a single breath. Such a deception is exceedingly deadly. The aura over there is sinister. We must not enter under any circumstances.”

p.src: Sanzang said, “If we cannot go in, I am truly famished.” Wukong said, “If you are truly hungry, Master, please dismount and sit here on this level ground while I go elsewhere to beg some food for you.” Sanzang dismounted as he was told, and Bajie took firm hold of the reins. Sha Monk put down the luggage, opened the bundle, took out the alms bowl, and handed it to Wukong. Taking the bowl in hand, Wukong instructed Sha Monk, “Good brother, you must not go any farther. Guard Master well and keep him safely seated here. When I return with food, we shall continue westward.” Sha Monk assented. Wukong then said to Sanzang, “Master, this place promises little good and much ill. By no means move from here or go elsewhere. Old Sun is off to beg for food.” The Tang Monk said, “There is no need for more words. Just go quickly and return quickly. I shall wait for you here.” Wukong turned to leave, but came back again and said, “Master, I know you have little patience for sitting still, so I shall give you a means of keeping safe.” He took out his gold-banded cudgel, gave it a flourish, and drew a circle around the level ground, asking the Tang Monk to sit in the middle. He had Bajie and Sha Monk stand guard on either side, with the horse and luggage placed close at hand. With palms joined, he said to the Tang Monk, “This circle drawn by Old Sun is stronger than walls of bronze and iron. No tiger, leopard, wolf, crawling beast, demon, or fiend, whatever it may be, will dare come near. Only you must not step outside the circle. Sit calmly within it and I guarantee you will come to no harm. But if you leave the circle, you will surely fall victim to a deadly hand. Remember this above all—heed my earnest warning!” Sanzang obeyed, and master and disciples all sat down solemnly.

p.src: Wukong mounted the clouds and flew south in search of a village where he might beg food. Before long he saw ancient trees towering into the sky, and beneath them stood a country settlement. He lowered his cloud and looked closely. This is what he saw:

He lowered his cloud and looked closely. This is what he saw:

p.src: As Wukong strolled along observing the village, he heard a creak from a brushwood gate. An old man emerged, dragging a staff of goosefoot wood. He wore a sheepskin cap, a ragged robe, and rush sandals. Leaning on his staff, he tilted his head toward the sky and said, “The northwest wind is rising; tomorrow will be fine.” Before he had finished speaking, a little pug dog ran out behind him and barked wildly at Wukong. Only then did the old man turn his head and see Wukong holding an alms bowl. Wukong saluted him and said, “Venerable benefactor, I am a monk commissioned by the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to journey to the Western Heaven, worship the Buddha, and seek the scriptures. We happen to be passing through your honoured district, and as my master is hungry, I have come specially to your esteemed residence to beg a vegetarian meal.” Hearing this, the old man nodded, struck his staff on the ground, and said, “Elder, forget about begging for food. You have taken the wrong road.” Wukong said, “I have not.” The old man said, “The main road to the Western Heaven lies due north of here. It is a thousand li from here. Why do you not go and find the main road?” Wukong laughed. “Due north is exactly where I came from. My master is sitting on the main road at this very moment, waiting for me to bring back food.” The old man said, “What nonsense this monk speaks! If your master is waiting on the main road for you to beg food, it would take six or seven days to walk the thousand li here and another six or seven days to return. Would he not starve to death?” Wukong laughed. “To tell you the truth, venerable benefactor, it has not yet been as long as it takes to drink a cup of hot tea since I left my master, and already I have reached this place. Once I have obtained some food, I must hurry back in time for the midday meal.”

p.src: At these words, the old man grew frightened and said to himself, “This monk is a ghost—a ghost!” He hurriedly turned and made for the house. Wukong seized him and said, “Where are you going, benefactor? If you have any food, quickly spare me some.” The old man said, “It is inconvenient, most inconvenient. Try another household.” Wukong said, “You truly do not know how to treat a guest. You say that I am a thousand li from my master. If I go on to another household, will that not mean another thousand li? My master really would starve to death!” The old man said, “To tell you the truth, there are six or seven mouths in my family, old and young alike. We have only just washed three sheng of rice and put it in the pot, and it is not yet cooked. Go and look elsewhere for a while, then come back.” Wukong said, “The ancients said, ‘Better to sit at one house than run to three.’ This poor monk will wait here for a while.” Seeing how persistently Wukong pestered him, the old man lost his temper, raised his goosefoot staff, and struck at him. Wukong showed no fear at all. The old man struck his bald head seven or eight times, but to him it was no more than having an itch scratched. The old man said, “This monk must have come here just to get his head beaten.” Wukong laughed. “Old sir, beat me as much as you like, but be sure to keep an exact count of the blows: one sheng of rice for every stroke. Measure it out at your leisure.” Hearing this, the old man hastily dropped his staff, ran inside, and shut the door, crying only, “A ghost! A ghost!” The whole family was thrown into such terror that they trembled from head to foot and barred both the front and rear doors.

p.src: When Pilgrim saw him shut the door, he thought to himself, “That old rogue just said he was washing rice to put in the pot, but who knows whether it was true or false? As the saying goes, ‘Daoists convert the worthy, while Buddhists convert the foolish.’ I had better go inside and see.” Our Great Sage formed a hand seal, performed an invisibility spell, and went straight into the kitchen. Sure enough, steam billowed from the pot, in which half a potful of dry-cooked rice was boiling. He thrust his alms bowl into it, scooped up a bowlful to the brim, then mounted a cloud and returned; of this no more need be said.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tang Sanzang sat inside the circle and waited a long while, but Pilgrim did not return. Rising slightly and gazing anxiously into the distance, he said, “Where has that monkey gone to beg for food?” Bajie laughed beside him and said, “Who knows where he has gone off amusing himself? What food is he begging for? He has merely left us imprisoned here.” Sanzang said, “Why do you call this being imprisoned?” Bajie said, “Master, you truly do not understand. The ancients drew a circle on the ground to make a prison. He drew this circle with his cudgel, and it is stronger than iron walls and bronze ramparts. But if tigers, wolves, or demon beasts come, how could it possibly hold them back? We could only let them eat us without resistance.” Sanzang said, “Wuneng, what do you think we should do?” Bajie replied, “This place neither shelters us from the wind nor keeps out the cold. If it were up to old Pig, we should simply follow the road and continue westward. Once Elder Brother has obtained food, he will surely come swiftly by cloud and catch up with us. If he has food, we can eat it before going on. We have sat here for a while now, and my feet are terribly cold!”

p.src: When Sanzang heard these words, it was as though the star of ill fortune had arrived. He yielded to the fool, and they all stepped outside the circle. Bajie led the horse, Sha Monk shouldered the luggage, and the elder walked forward along the road. Before long they reached the buildings, which proved to be a residence facing south with its back to the north. Outside the gate, whitewashed walls spread outward on both sides, and above it stood an inverted-lotus, measuring-cup gate tower, all adorned in five colors. The gate stood half open and half closed. Bajie tethered the horse to the stone drum beside the gatepost; Sha Monk set down the luggage; and Sanzang, afraid of the wind, sat on the threshold. Bajie said, “Master, this place looks like the mansion of a duke or marquis, or the household of a minister. There is no one outside the front gate; they must all be warming themselves by the fire within. You sit here while I go inside and have a look.” Tang Sanzang said, “Be careful, and do not offend the household.” The fool replied, “I understand. Since embracing the true Buddhist path, I have learned some manners along the way. I am no longer like some uncouth rustic.”

p.src: The fool tucked his rake into his belt, straightened his blue brocade robe, and walked through the gate with an air of refinement. He saw a great hall three bays wide, its latticed curtains raised high. It was utterly silent, with no trace of anyone and not even a table, chair, or household utensil. Passing around the screen gate and continuing inward, he came to a passage hall. Behind the hall stood a large upper-story building. One of its latticed windows was half open, and through it he could dimly see a canopy of yellow silk. The fool said, “Someone must still be sleeping because of the cold.” Without regard for whether it was an outer or inner chamber, he strode directly upstairs. When he lifted the curtain with his hand and looked inside, the sight frightened him into staggering backward. For on the ivory bed within the canopy lay a ghastly white heap of bones: the skull was as large as a bushel basket, and the leg bones were four or five feet long. The fool steadied himself, but could not stop the tears from falling down his cheeks. Nodding toward the skeleton, he sighed, “Little did you know that—

p.src: Just as Bajie was lamenting, he saw a flicker of firelight behind the canopy. The fool said, “There must be someone tending the incense and offerings behind there.” He hurried around the canopy to look, but it was only light shining through a window in the passage connecting the upper rooms. On that side stood a brightly lacquered table, across which several pieces of brocade-padded clothing had been carelessly draped. When the fool picked them up to examine them, they proved to be three brocade-quilted waistcoats.

p.src: Without caring whether it was right or wrong, he took them downstairs, passed out through the hall, and went straight to the gate, saying, “Master, there is not a soul in this place. It is a house of the dead. Old Pig went inside and climbed all the way to the upper floor, where there was a heap of bones within a yellow silk canopy. Beside the passage through the upper rooms were three brocade-quilted waistcoats, which I have brought here. This too is a little piece of good fortune on our journey. The weather is cold now, so they are just what we need. Master, take off your short robe for the moment and wear one underneath. Enjoy its warmth and spare yourself the cold.” Sanzang said, “You must not, you must not. The monastic rules say, ‘Taking openly and taking secretly are both theft.’ If someone should discover this and pursue us, then bring us before the authorities, we would certainly be convicted of theft. Take them back at once and drape them where they originally lay. We shall sit here awhile out of the wind, then set out when Wukong returns. Those who have left the household must not covet petty gains like this.” Bajie said, “There is no one in sight in any direction; not even the chickens and dogs know of it. Only we know, so who could accuse me? What evidence could there be? It is just as if we had found them. Why quibble over open taking or secret taking?” Sanzang said, “You are behaving recklessly! Though people may not know, how could it be hidden from Heaven? The Dark Emperor admonished, ‘Though conscience is betrayed in a darkened room, the eyes of the gods flash like lightning.’ Hurry and return them. Do not covet things to which you have no rightful claim.”

p.src: The fool had no intention of listening. He smiled at Tang Sanzang and said, “Master, since becoming a man I have worn several waistcoats, but never have I seen any quilted with brocade like these. If you will not wear one, let old Pig try one on, enjoy the novelty, and warm his back. When Elder Brother returns, I shall take it off, put it back, and continue the journey.” Sha Monk said, “If that is what you propose, I shall wear one too.” The two of them took off their outer robes together and slipped on the waistcoats. No sooner had they tightened the ties than, for some unknown reason, they could no longer stand steadily and fell to the ground with a thud. Those waistcoats proved even more effective than expert binders: in an instant they pinned both men's arms behind their backs and bound them tightly against their bodies. Sanzang stamped his feet and lamented in alarm. He hurried over to untie them, but there was no way he could loosen the bonds. The three of them kept shouting without cease, and their cries soon alerted the demon chief.

No sooner had they tightened the ties than, for some unknown reason, they could no longer stand steadily and fell to the ground with a thud.
Those waistcoats proved even more effective than expert binders: in an instant they pinned both men's arms behind their backs and bound them tightly against their bodies.
Sanzang stamped his feet and lamented in alarm. He hurried over to untie them, but there was no way he could loosen the bonds.
The three of them kept shouting without cease, and their cries soon alerted the demon chief.

p.src: It turned out that the mansion had indeed been conjured by the monster, who used it every day to capture travelers. As he sat in his cave, he suddenly heard cries of resentment. He hurried outside to look and saw that several people had indeed been bound. The demon summoned his underlings, went with them to the spot, and dispelled the form of the towers and chambers. They seized Tang Sanzang, led away the white horse, shouldered the luggage, and carried Bajie and Sha Seng off to the cave as well. The old demon mounted the dais and sat in state, while the lesser demons pushed Tang Sanzang before it and forced him to kneel prostrate on the ground. The demon asked, “What land are you monks from? How dare you steal my clothes in broad daylight?” Sanzang answered tearfully, “This poor monk is an imperial envoy of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, bound for the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. As I was hungry, I sent my eldest disciple to beg for food, but he had not yet returned. We failed to heed his words and mistakenly entered your immortal abode to shelter from the wind. Unexpectedly, these two disciples of mine coveted the trifles they saw and brought the garments out. I would never harbor any wicked intent and told them to return everything to its proper place. They ignored me and insisted on putting them on to warm their backs, never imagining that they would fall into Your Majesty’s trap and bring about my capture. I beseech Your Majesty to show mercy and spare my wretched life, that I may obtain the true scriptures. I shall remember your kindness forever and proclaim it through the Eastern Land for a thousand ages.” The demon laughed. “I have often heard it said that anyone who eats a piece of Tang Sanzang’s flesh will see white hair turn black and fallen teeth grow anew. Now fortune has brought you here uninvited, and still you expect me to spare you! What is the name of that eldest disciple of yours? Where did he go to beg for food?” Hearing this, Bajie immediately spoke up boastfully: “My elder brother is none other than Sun Wukong, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, who caused havoc in Heaven five hundred years ago.”

Saying nothing aloud, he thought to himself, “I have long heard that fellow possesses vast magical powers, and now we have met quite unexpectedly.” He ordered, “Underlings, bind Tang Sanzang. Take the enchanted treasures off the other two, replace them with two ropes, and bind them as well. Carry them to the rear for now. Once I have captured their eldest disciple, we shall wash them all together and steam them in one cage to eat.” The lesser demons acknowledged the order, bound all three men, and carried them to the rear. They tethered the white horse at the manger and carried the luggage inside. All the demons sharpened their weapons and prepared to capture the Pilgrim, but we shall say no more of them for now.

p.src: Now Sun the Pilgrim had taken a bowlful of vegetarian food from a household in a southern village. Riding his cloud back along the old route, he came straight to the level ground on the mountainside and lowered his cloud, only to find Tang Sanzang gone, with no notion where he had gone. The circle he had drawn with his staff was still there, but both men and horse had vanished. Looking back toward the mansion, he found that it too had completely vanished; there were only grotesque rocks at the foot of the mountain. Startled, the Pilgrim thought, “There is no need to ask—they must have fallen into that monster’s cruel hands.” He hurriedly followed the hoofprints along the road and gave chase toward the west.

p.src: After traveling five or six li, just as he was overcome with sorrow, he heard voices beyond the northern slope. When he looked, he saw an old man wrapped in a felt coat, a warm cap covering his head, a pair of half-new, half-worn oiled boots on his feet, and a dragon-headed staff in his hand. Behind him followed a young servant carrying a broken sprig of wintersweet, while the old man walked before the slope chanting a song. The Pilgrim set down his bowl, saluted the old man face-to-face, and said, “Good elder, this poor monk offers his greetings.” The old man immediately returned the salute and asked, “Where have you come from, venerable monk?” The Pilgrim replied, “We come from the Eastern Land and are going to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Our company consists of master and three disciples. Because my master was hungry, I went especially to beg for food, leaving the other three seated on the level part of that slope to await me. When I returned, they were gone, and I do not know which road they took. May I ask whether you happened to see them?” Hearing this, the old man gave a cold chuckle and said, “Among those three, was there one with a long snout and great ears?” The Pilgrim said, “Yes, yes, yes.” “And was there another with a dark, ill-favored face, leading a white horse and accompanying a plump, fair-faced monk?” The Pilgrim said, “Yes, yes, yes.” The old man said, “You took the wrong road. Do not look for them; each of you should save his own life.” The Pilgrim replied, “The fair-faced one is my master, and those strange-looking fellows are my junior disciples. Together we made a devout vow to fetch the scriptures from the Western Heaven. How could I fail to seek them?” The old man said, “When I passed this way just now, I saw them take the wrong path and blunder into a demon’s jaws.” The Pilgrim said, “Please instruct me, good elder. What sort of demon is it? Where does it live? I shall go to its door, reclaim my companions, and continue to the Western Heaven.” The old man said, “This mountain is called Golden Pouch Mountain. Before the mountain is a cave called Golden Pouch Cave, and within it dwells the Great King One-Horned Rhinoceros. That great king possesses vast magical powers and tremendous martial might. Your three companions are certainly doomed this time. If you go looking for them, I fear even your own life will not be safe; you would do better not to go. I dare neither stop you nor detain you; you must weigh the matter for yourself.”

p.src: The Pilgrim bowed twice in thanks and said, “Many thanks for your guidance, good elder. How could I possibly not go in search of them?” He poured out the vegetarian food for the old man and prepared to put away the empty bowl himself. The old man set down his staff, took the bowl, and passed it to the servant. Then both revealed their true forms, knelt, and kowtowed, saying, “Great Sage, we minor gods dare conceal nothing from you. We are the mountain god and the local earth god of this mountain, and we have been waiting here to receive you. We shall keep the food together with the bowl, so that you may travel unburdened and freely exercise your powers. Once you have rescued Tang Sanzang from his peril, we shall present the food to him, thus displaying your perfect reverence and filial devotion.” The Pilgrim shouted, “You hairy wretches deserve a beating! Since you knew I was coming, why did you not greet me sooner? Why hide your heads and show your tails like this? What is the meaning of it?” The earth god replied, “The Great Sage is quick-tempered. We minor gods dared not act rashly, for fear of offending your august countenance, and therefore assumed disguises to inform you.” His anger abating, the Pilgrim said, “I shall remember that I owe you a beating. Keep my bowl safe and sound while I go and capture that monster.” The earth god and mountain god respectfully obeyed.

p.src: The band of little demons hurried into the cave and reported, “Your Majesty, out front there is a monk with a hairy face and a jutting mouth. He calls himself Sun Wukong, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and has come to demand the return of his master.” When the demon king heard this, he was delighted and said, “I have been hoping he would come. Since leaving my own palace and descending to the mortal world, I have not once had the chance to test my martial skill. Now that he has come today, he is sure to prove a worthy opponent.” He immediately ordered the little demons to bring out his weapon. Every demon in the cave, great and small, sprang eagerly into action and carried out a steel-tipped spear twelve feet long, which they handed to the old monster. The old monster issued his command: “Underlings, see that your ranks are in good order. Those who advance shall be rewarded; those who retreat shall be put to death!” Receiving the order, the demons followed the old monster out through the entrance and shouted, “Which one of you is Sun Wukong?”

p.src: The Great Sage Sun stepped forward and said, “Your Grandpa Sun is right here! Hurry and return my master, and neither side need suffer harm; but if you utter so much as half a ‘no,’ I shall leave you without a place to bury your corpse!” The demon roared, “You insolent, wretched monkey-spirit! What powers do you possess, that you dare make such an outrageous boast?” The Pilgrim said, “You vile creature! It seems you have never witnessed what Old Sun can do.” The demon said, “Your master stole my clothes. I did indeed seize him, and now I mean to steam and eat him. What manner of hero are you, to dare come to my door and demand him back?” The Pilgrim said, “My master is a loyal, virtuous, and upright monk. How could he possibly steal anything belonging to a demon like you?” The demon said, “Beside the mountain road I conjured up an immortal’s manor. Your master slipped inside, succumbed to greed and desire, and secretly put on three brocade and padded waistcoats of mine. He was caught with the stolen goods upon him, and that is why I seized him. If you truly possess ability, then match your strength against mine. If you can withstand me for three rounds, I shall spare your master’s life; but if you cannot, I shall send you straight down the road to the netherworld.”

p.src: The two fought for thirty rounds without either gaining the upper hand. When the demon king saw that Sun Wukong’s staff-work was precise and orderly, with not the slightest opening in either attack or withdrawal, he was so delighted that he repeatedly cried in admiration, “Fine monkey! Fine monkey! You truly possess the skill of the one who caused havoc in Heaven.” The Great Sage, for his part, admired the demon’s unerring spear-work: warding off blows on the right and blocking them on the left, he displayed a wealth of skill. He too called out, “Fine demon! Fine demon! You are indeed a demon chief capable of stealing the elixir.” The two fought another ten or twenty rounds. Then the demon king touched the point of his spear to the ground and shouted an order for all the little demons to attack together. Those vicious monsters came one after another, wielding sabers and staves, gripping swords and brandishing spears, until they had the Great Sage Sun surrounded in their midst. The Pilgrim showed not the slightest fear and merely cried, “Well come! Well come! This is exactly to my liking.” With his compliant golden-hooped staff, he met attacks from the front and parried those from behind, blocking to the east and sweeping enemies from the west. Yet that horde of demons showed no intention of retreating. At last the Pilgrim lost patience. He tossed his golden-hooped staff into the air and shouted, “Transform!” At once it changed into hundreds upon thousands of iron staves, like flying serpents and darting pythons, raining chaotically from every part of the sky. At the sight, every one of the demons was frightened out of his wits. Hunching their shoulders and ducking their heads, they all fled into the cave for their lives. The old demon king gave a cold chuckle and said, “Do not be insolent, monkey. Behold my power!” He quickly took from his sleeve a gleaming, cold-white ring, tossed it into the air, and cried, “Strike!” With a sudden whoosh, it gathered the golden-hooped staff back into one and slipped around it, carrying it away. The Great Sage Sun was left barehanded and weaponless, and had to escape with his life by turning a somersault. The demon returned victorious to his cave, while the Pilgrim, dazed and bewildered, knew not what to do. Exactly so:
